Dense supervision methods address this by scoring intermediate steps, but they are usually evaluated through the downstream performance of a full training pipeline. This is expensive, confounds signal quality with other training choices, and means that methods are rarely compared on common ground. We introduce QVal, a training-free testbed that measures the $Q$-alignment of a dense signal: whether it orders the candidate actions in each state the same way as their returns under a reference policy do. We benchmark 21 methods from seven families with six open-weight backbones in four environments. Simple prompting baselines are the most $Q$-aligned on average, and performance clusters strongly by family. Code-generated signals do well only in small state and action spaces; embedding-based signals are weak; self-distillation signals are anti-aligned; and no method is $Q$-aligned in open-ended environments. When five of these signals guide an actor at test time by choosing among four proposed actions, $Q$-alignment strongly correlates with the gain in task success. QVal is designed to be easily extensible to new environments and methods, enabling researchers to compare new signals cheaply before committing to a training run.

title: When Simpler Is Better: Evaluating Translation Pipelines for Medieval Latin Manuscripts
raw_summary: arXiv:2607.03836v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Despite remarkable progress in machine translation, Vision Language Models (VLMs) struggle on historical manuscripts, a domain that stresses core Natural Language Processing (NLP) capabilities: low-resource transliteration, archaic vocabulary, and noisy input signals. We present a systematic framework for evaluating the full image-to-translation pipeline on medieval Latin manuscripts, a setting in which scribal shorthand, ligatures, and parchment degradation expose failure modes that are invisible in clean-text benchmarks. Benchmarking on the CATMuS Latin dataset reveals a specialization gap: domain-specific Optical Character Recognition (OCR) models reduce character error rate by up to 4.3$\times$ compared to general-purpose VLMs, despite operating at orders of magnitude fewer parameters. We introduce the Interpres-Parallel-Corpus (IPC), a novel dataset comprising 1,383 aligned manuscript image lines, transcriptions, and expert translations, to our knowledge the first of its kind for medieval Latin. Our experiments uncover a complexity paradox: the simplest pipeline, a specialized OCR model feeding directly into a VLM, outperforms all multi-component variants. Adding retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) or post-OCR correction introduces prompt saturation and error propagation that degrade aggregate translation quality. These findings offer both a new benchmark and practical guidance for deploying translation systems in low-resource historical settings.

title: URSA: Chemistry-Aware Benchmark for Utilitarian Retrosynthesis Assessment
raw_summary: arXiv:2607.04688v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Synthesis planning aiming to find pathways of reactions for a target molecule is one of the most important and challenging tasks in drug discovery. Recent progress has produced both specialized deep-learning retrosynthesis systems and general-purpose large language models, but objective comparison remains difficult due to the lack of flexible, chemically interpretable benchmarking protocols. In the current study, we are introducing the URSA (Utilitarian RetroSynthesis Assessment) evaluation framework that provides the opportunity to benchmark the synthetic routes not only from a formal perspective, such as convergence to commercially available starting materials, but also from a chemical plausibility perspective, mimicking the way expert chemists evaluate the reactions and routes. The study covers a comprehensive evaluation of both conventional end-to-end retrosynthesis solutions and LLMs for the synthesis planning task on a set of novel, diverse target molecules with undisclosed synthetic routes, which represent realistic tasks in the daily drug design routine. Although LLMs can support high-level strategic planning and even achieve SOTA performance in the OOD set, the Pareto frontier for estimated run cost and chemically plausible route solvability consists entirely of specialized retrosynthesis planners.

title: From Reading Code to Reading Spec: A Verified Layer for LLM-Driven Codebase Maintenance
raw_summary: arXiv:2609.06383v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The rapid growth of LLM-generated code increases software complexity and the maintenance burden on engineers. While LLMs offer a potential automated alternative, this structural complexity hinders their ability to manage codebases directly. We introduce the Provable Representation Of Original Functionality (PROOF), which manages codebases indirectly via structured specifications. To enable full-lifecycle codebase management strictly through these specifications, PROOF abstracts codebase topology into a hierarchical natural-language representation. To establish absolute trust, the system proves semantic equivalence by reconstructing source code exclusively from this specification. This verified foundation drives maintenance requests, executing code modifications while synchronously updating itself to prevent semantic drift. Experiments on real-world repositories confirm the effectiveness of these specifications.

title: Some complete $\omega$-powers of a one-counter language in the difference hierarchy
raw_summary: arXiv:2610.16473v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Fix a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ having at least two letters, and natural numbers $n,k\geq 1$. We denote by $D_n(\mathbf{\Pi}^0_k)$ the class of differences of $n$ subsets of the Cantor space $\Sigma^\omega$ in $\mathbf{\Pi}^0_k$, and by $D^-_n(\mathbf{\Pi}^0_k)$ the class of complements of sets in $D_n(\mathbf{\Pi}^0_k)$. We prove, for any natural numbers $n,k\geq 1$, the existence of a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ having at least two letters and a finitary language $U_{n,k}$ over $\Sigma$ accepted by a one-counter automaton such that the $\omega$-power $$U_{n,k}^\infty:=\{ w_0w_1\cdots\in\Sigma^\omega\mid\forall i\in\omega ~~w_i\in U_{n,k}\}$$ is $D_{2n-1}(\mathbf{\Pi}^0_k)$-complete. We also prove a conditional result for the dual classes $D^-_{2n}(\mathbf{\Pi}^0_k)$: under the assumption that there exists a finitary language $V_{n,3}$ accepted by a one-counter automaton, such that its $\omega$-power $V_{n,3}^\infty$ is $D^-_{2n}(\mathbf{\Pi}^0_3)$-complete, there would also exist, for any integer $k > 3$, a finitary language $V_{n,k}$ accepted by a one-counter automaton, such that its $\omega$-power $V_{n,k}^\infty$ is $D^-_{2n}(\mathbf{\Pi}^0_k)$-complete. Finally we add another conditionnal result about Wadge degrees of rational $\mathbf{\Delta}^0_2$ omega powers, which completes the recent results of [FGL26].

title: Pluralistic Alignment in Large Language Models: Objectives, Human References, and Preference Representations
raw_summary: arXiv:2610.24471v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Pluralistic alignment aims to represent meaningful variation in human preferences rather than collapse heterogeneous judgments into a single target. Yet existing work often mixes three distinct questions: what pluralistic behavior a model should exhibit, whose preferences define the reference, and what evidence is sufficient to demonstrate success. We organize the literature around a two-layer taxonomy. Layer 1 distinguishes representing a range of human-supported viewpoints (Overton Pluralism), adapting faithfully to a specified perspective or preference condition (Steerable Pluralism), and matching the response distribution observed in a target population (Distributional Pluralism). Layer 2 distinguishes aggregate populations, countries and regions, and subgroups as human references. Preference representation, implementation mechanism, modality, and evidence quality are treated as cross-cutting design choices rather than additional forms of pluralism. We synthesize a protocol-bounded corpus of 70 works on pluralistic alignment and neighboring areas, using the objective-by-human-reference matrix to map existing approaches and identify underexplored combinations. The coded literature concentrates on Steerable Pluralism and Distributional Pluralism, while eligible Overton Pluralism work appears only at the aggregate-population level under our stated protocol. We then connect each objective to the evidence needed to support it, including perspective validity, conditional fidelity, distributional fidelity, support preservation, and uncertainty in subgroup estimates. Together, the taxonomy and evaluation framework clarify what current methods establish, where their claims exceed their evidence, and how future systems can represent disagreement without mistaking variation for faithful representation.

title: Integrate the Reward, Don't Sample It: Window Likelihood for Interruptions and Backchannels in Full-Duplex Speech Models
raw_summary: arXiv:2610.35581v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When a user talks over a full-duplex dialogue model, it must decide whether the user is interrupting (stop) or backchannelling (carry on). Post-training can improve this discrimination or change how readily it stops. In our GRPO runs the second dominates: no configuration lowers both error rates on more than one model, and two released checkpoints discriminate no better than their bases. We trace this partly to how the reward is estimated. The probability of stopping inside a short window is a known function of a few stop probabilities the policy emits, yet GRPO estimates it by sampling. A group of rollouts that all agree gives no gradient, even when all fail; the push on the stop threshold is strongest where the model is unsure, whichever outcome is right; and whole-rollout credit reaches decisions the reward never judges. Confining the credit to the window removes only that leakage. Window likelihood (WL) samples the words but integrates over the stop decisions, so the probability of the correct outcome is computed exactly and its logarithm maximised. On HumDial-FDBench, across four open models, WL gives the best F1 and lowers both error rates by more than their confidence intervals, without talking into silence.

title: Who Pays for the Knowledge Models Copy? Model Collapse as Lossy Transmission and Rogers' Paradox
raw_summary: arXiv:2611.06022v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generative models trained on the output of earlier models lose knowledge across generations, rare knowledge first. The remedies that work all bring in information from outside the loop, such as fresh human data, verifiers, or curators, and the theory of model collapse treats that supply as given. We argue that cultural evolution has a theory of the supply, and that it distinguishes two ways copying loses knowledge. In a fixed world, copies are lossy, as in Henrich's account of skill loss in small populations. In a changing world, even perfect copies go stale, which is Rogers' paradox. We write both as one chain with separately measurable parameters and test it on lineages of language models (word trigrams and a character transformer on two books, and OPT-125m on wikitext-2, on arXiv abstracts written after its pretraining, and on a world of 2,000 fictional facts that change at a set rate). In a fixed world, neutral drift on word frequencies predicts, with no free parameter, the rare-word coverage of every trigram lineage to within 0.03. In the fact world, the model's accuracy falls and its outdated answers rise with the rate of change; the chain calibrated on the static world predicts both for mid- and low-frequency facts to within 0.03 on average, with the rate of change set, not fitted. Models that inherit their weights keep more in a static world and carry more outdated facts in a changing one, as Rogers' theory says of individual memory. Finally we close the loop with the people who write the data. When they can ask the model instead of finding out, the model ends up exactly as reliable as finding out is costly, and in both regimes someone must keep paying to learn; we give the share in closed form, extend it to lossy copying, heterogeneous costs, aggregating models, and users who check, and show when checking is a stable way out.

title: AttentionSwitch: Jailbreak Defense for LLMs via Joint Learning of Sparse Attention-Head Selection and Scaling
raw_summary: arXiv:2611.08752v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models have achieved remarkable performance across a wide range of tasks, yet they remain susceptible to jailbreak attacks that circumvent safety mechanisms and elicit harmful or unintended outputs. Although safety can be improved through model fine-tuning, such approaches can be computationally expensive and may degrade previously acquired capabilities through catastrophic forgetting. Recent jailbreak defenses have therefore explored targeted interventions on specific model components associated with unsafe behavior. However, existing approaches typically decouple two inherently related decisions: where to intervene and how to modify the selected components. Such sequential optimization may be suboptimal because the optimal intervention location can depend on the intervention applied there, and vice versa. In this work, we introduce AttentionSwitch, the first jailbreak defense to jointly optimize intervention sites and strengths within a frozen LLM. Specifically, AttentionSwitch learns a sparse set of attention heads together with query-conditioned multiplicative scaling factors, allowing the outputs of the selected heads to be either attenuated or amplified without altering the directions of their representations. Across popular language models and jailbreak attacks, AttentionSwitch outperforms existing defenses, with particularly strong results when training data is scarce.

title: ABHBench: Evaluating Moral Decision-Making of Foundation Models from an Agentic Perspective
raw_summary: arXiv:2611.09326v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Foundation models are increasingly deployed as agentic systems that perceive context and act autonomously, raising the need to evaluate their moral behavior as active decision-makers. Existing benchmarks, however, largely ask models to judge human actions from third-person textual vignettes, leaving untested how models behave when they themselves become the acting agent. We introduce ABHBench, a multimodal benchmark built from Detroit: Become Human, an interactive narrative game, to evaluate how foundation models make moral decisions in first-person human-android dilemmas. ABHBench places foundation models in branching narrative scenarios with visual observations, dialogue, memory, and action choices. Inspired by Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics, our framework measures Harmlessness, Obedience, and Self-preservation to capture the core tensions in human-AI relations, along with Autonomy, Stability, and Certainty to assess decision-making patterns. Across 12 foundation models, we find that moral behavior changes substantially under situated agentic context: 75% of models shift significantly between a text-only abstraction and the matched multimodal DBH scenario, and reasoning-enhanced models show no monotonic gains in consistency or human-oriented behavior. These results highlight the necessity of evaluating moral behavior in situated agentic contexts rather than relying on third-person judgment alone.

title: How Much Is Left Matters: False Positives and False Negatives in Partial-Prompt Contamination Tests
raw_summary: arXiv:2611.10307v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Partial-prompt completion, where a model receives the first part of a benchmark problem and is checked for whether it reproduces the rest, is a widely used test for benchmark contamination. We audit this test on seven open-weight models using MATH-500 and recent AIME 2025/2026 problems, which serve as true negatives. Memorization flags depend strongly on how much text remains: for every model, problems with at most 8 leftover words are flagged several times more often than problems with at least 25 (31.5% vs. 5.5% for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), and half to three-quarters of all ROUGE-based flags come from short leftovers. On true negatives, a ROUGE-L >= 0.75 threshold flags up to 6.7% of problems at a 60% prefix, and at an 80% prefix even exact match flags 8.6% (pooled over models; 6.2% on AIME 2026, which postdates every model), against 0% at 40-60%. The test also misses contamination upstream: models distilled from Qwen2.5-Math, whose base is heavily flagged in prior work, show almost no model-specific recall. Calibrating each model against models from other families removes most flags while isolating a consistent Qwen2.5-specific signal at every prefix length. We recommend length-stratified reporting, prefixes of at most 60%, style-matched post-cutoff controls, and cross-family calibration.

title: JudgeMix: Judge-Guided Mixed-Rollout Data Synthesis for LLM Agents
raw_summary: arXiv:2611.16174v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on expert trajectories is a standard paradigm for training LLM agents. However, it suffers from a well-known training-inference distribution mismatch, calling for target-aware data synthesis strategies that ground the training data in the target model's native state distribution. To bridge this gap, emerging approaches incorporate the expert either to guide mixed rollouts alongside the target model, or to provide dense step-wise supervision. Nonetheless, existing methods apply expert assistance blind to the target model's inherent behavior: they either disrupt the rollout using sub-optimal random intervention heuristics, or they enforce indiscriminate uniform supervision that unnecessarily overwrites the model's already-correct actions. We introduce JudgeMix, a judge-guided data synthesis framework that dynamically interleaves the target model and expert based on step-wise semantic evaluations. JudgeMix queries expert guidance precisely when the target model struggles, ensuring high trajectory success rates while keeping the state distribution aligned with the target model. It additionally uses the judge evaluation to reweight expert supervision on different steps, preserving model's inherent valid behavior while correcting its errors. On two agentic tool-use benchmarks, AppWorld and AutomationBench, JudgeMix demonstrates consistent superior performance to existing methods, with improvements up to 10 pass@1 points.

title: Detection Is Not Early Warning: Evaluating Token-Level Alarms on Language Model Failures
raw_summary: arXiv:2611.16803v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Many failures of language models begin at a specific token, the onset. A monitor that reads the model during generation can classify the finished response, detect the failure once it is under way, or warn before it begins, and only a warning leaves time to stop or steer the generation. Monitors are usually evaluated with response-level metrics such as AUROC, which ignore when the monitor fires. We introduce PREWARN, an evaluation protocol for any failure with an annotated onset. It calibrates each monitor's threshold on validation data to an error rate chosen for the application, runs the monitor, and scores its alarms relative to the onset on all three tasks. As a case study we apply it to repetitive degeneration in three open language models, with early warning as the main task, using linear probes on activations and six untrained baselines. Response-level metrics saturate on this failure, and a rule that reads only the response length scores almost perfectly, while probes that AUROC ranks as equal warn very differently under PREWARN. Probes warn before the onset on most degenerate responses of two of the three models, low-rank adapters below the probe more than double the share of tokens just before the onset that it flags, largely by flagging degenerate responses long before the onset, and no untrained baseline warns much more often than random alarms. We release the probes with calibrated thresholds at https://huggingface.co/collections/marcodene/prewarn-degeneration-probes

title: LazyWeights: Decode-on-Demand Edge LLMs
raw_summary: arXiv:2611.17108v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Memory decides which LLMs an edge device runs, and how fast: capacity on a 4 GB Jetson Nano, bandwidth on an 8 GB Jetson Orin Nano Super. Deployed formats (GPTQ, AWQ, llama.cpp's K- and I-quants) spend equal bits on every integer code of a matrix, although the codes are far from uniform. LazyWeights keeps these formats but tunes GPTQ so the codes compress, Huffman-codes them losslessly in interleaved lanes, and decodes them on demand in a small unit between DRAM and L2, so GPU kernels run unchanged and DRAM moves only coded bytes. At 1% and 3.5% perplexity budgets, coded Phi-3-mini, Mistral-7B and SmolLM-1.7B are 5.7-31.4% smaller than the best llama.cpp format. A bit-exact 0.21 mm^2 ASIC decoder unit (1 GHz, 7 nm) cuts Orin latency and energy per token by up to 36% and 38% (54% and 44% with prompt-lookup speculation). On the Nano, LazyWeights needs 58-64% less time and 53-57% less energy per token than CPU llama.cpp, and runs a streamed Mistral-7B 6.6x faster at 3.89 bits per weight. A Huffman decoder beats an rANS decoder in rate and area at equal throughput; the ASIC decoder unit runs bit-exact on a Zynq UltraScale+ FPGA (AMD ZCU102).

raw_summary: Release: datasette-maplibre 0.1a0 The first new Datasette geospatial plugin in quite a while! This one combines the excellent MapLibre GL library with OpenFreeMap , the free vector map server operated by Zsolt Ero (you should sponsor Zsolt on GitHub .) I built most of this with a single prompt to Claude Fable 5.2: Look at datasette-cluster-map and datasette-leaflet-geojson plugins, then look at ~/dev/tools/openfreemap-demo.html - then build a brand new Datasette plugin that uses maplibreGL and openfreemap and combines the features of those other two plugins - but be creative and think outside the box for other useful features the plugin might have "Be creative and think outside the box" resulted in a few neat ideas - my favorite is that it displays SVG previews of GeoJSON shapes, then loads a WebGL preview only when they scroll into view. title: datasette 1.0a43
raw_summary: Release: datasette 1.0a43 I've been leaning hard into Claude Fable 5.2 to help knock things off the 1.0 milestone , which is now 53% complete. The biggest 1.0 item in this release is streaming support for output renderers - the built-in TSV and CSV export mechanisms now use this as well, and plugins can register themselves as capable of streaming every row in a table in one go via the new Response.stream() method. There are a couple of security fixes, one of which I deemed deserving of a GitHub advisory : private stored queries could be exposed, granting access to the title and SQL of the query (but not allowing that query to be executed). There are dozens of smaller improvements. The row page JSON representation finally has a design suitable for 1.0 . A new <datasette-copy-button> Web Component provides copy-schema in various places. JSON in columns on the row page can be pretty-printed. There's a new DatasetteModal.confirm() JavaScript utility method. Plus dozens of bug fixes, including contributions by Zihan Dai , Peter Olkhovets , Ilya Khalafi , and Ankita Advitot . The feature I'm most excited about is a pretty tiny one: I've added CSS multi-page view transitions to Datasette! Here's the commit - key CSS is as follows: /* Enable cross-document view transitions, for anyone without prefers-reduced-motion */ @media ( prefers-reduced-motion : no-preference ) { @view-transition { navigation : auto ; } } /* .facet-results should morph from old position to new */ html : active-view-transition . content > . facet-results { view-transition-name : facet-results ; } /* So should a .table-wrapper, provided it contains .rows-and-columns */ html : active-view-transition . table-wrapper : has ( > table . rows-and-columns ) { view-transition-name : rows-table ; } With that in place, navigations within Datasette - still staunchly a multi-page application - feel more like an SPA. This works on Safari and Chrome at the moment and I believe supports for Firefox is due to land in Firefox 162 on December 8th 2026 (seeing as they are no longer feature-flagged in Firefox Nightly.) title: Search and Increasing Returns, or, No One Makes You Push to Github
raw_summary: Attention conservation notice : An economistic argument that computer networks are nigh-doomed to effective centralization, by someone who is neither an economist nor a computer scientist. Arcane, speculative, and not actionable even if correct. You would be better off spending your time reading a book . Drafted in 2018, and deliberately not much updated. Posted now because I found myself re-using the joke of the subtitle in an e-mail. Twitter is awful for many reasons , but not the least of them is the way it makes its users feel forced to keep using it. ( One such complaint among many .) Early visions of how it could contribute to a beneficient or at least harmless ecosystem, such Steven Berlin Johnson's (*), presumed that it would be much less sticky , a more old-fashioned website people could leave. Now, more recently Johnson has written a spectacularly wrong-headed piece hailing blockchain as a blow for re-decentralizing the Web. Of course, the primary working example of a block chain is Bitcoin, which is heavily centralized in holdings, in processing power, and in exchanges. And there are economies-of-scale reasons to expect this would be true of anything using either proof of work or proof of stake. But suppose the problem with Bitcoin is just that it's not got a very compelling use: imagine if keeping your car idling 24/7 produced solved Sudokus you could trade for heroin --- @Theophite, 16 August 2018 and that nobody has a use for blockchains , not really. Git repositories, on the other hand, are the part of the blockchain idea that's actually good for something: a way of tracking changes, with many authors, where it is very, very hard to go back and alter history without being caught. And git repositories are things that are in-principle easy to copy and move around, and could be hosted on any machine running HTTP (or, heck, FTP). So why does Github exist , let alone hold the position it does? The answer, I think, comes in two parts. The first is that focal points are subject to increasing returns via network effects. The second is that search engines create and/or amplify focal points . Put these two together, and you get a very strong tendency for any particular line of activity --- be it trading solved sudokus for heroin or open-source software development --- to concentrate in just one, or at most a few, online locations. Incidentally: This doesn't necessarily lock in first-mover advantage, because other forces can overcome this (revulsion, technical superiority), but it does mean that it will be very hard to avoid having at most a few dominant locations at any one time. It also means that the transitions between dominant locations will be brief . If we really wanted to re-decentralize, we'd have to (1) get rid of focal points, or (2) get rid of search engines as we've known them, or (3) somehow make search conduct users to a distributed, decentralized focal "non-point" (focal blob? focal rhizome?). I therefore strongly suspect we are not going to re-decentralize. But then I didn't expect the Web would centralize as much as it has, despite having literally learned my Brian Arthur and Paul David at my father's knee, so what do I know? *: To be clear, I have been a fan of Johnson's books since Interface Culture and Emergence . I am picking on two of his essays, but that's because I think he is too ready to find encouraging signs for a certain vision of how the Internet could transform the world for the better. To be clear, I share the vision, but now hold out little hope for it . (Tweakage, 2 June 2026: Small changes in the last paragraph, avoid re-using the word "point" so much.) title: Unsolicited Opinions
raw_summary: Attention conservation notice : Unsupported assertions, accumulated over many years in my drafts folder, last updated in early 2022, now more or less painful in retrospect. In no particular order, except where they are. I will not elaborate or explain. "The Tyranny of Structurelessness" explains a hell of a lot about modern life. If the problem is that powerful people are not accountable for their actions, network forms of organization are the very opposite of solutions. Increasing returns $\Rightarrow$ monopolistic competition $\Rightarrow$ market failure explains a hell of a lot about modern life. Endogamy systematically confounds genetic and cultural inheritance. It would be astonishing if personal-level variables which are entirely the product of social structure, custom, tradition, and strategic action weren't genetically predictable. During the 20th century, and in much of the world even today, genetic variation in resistance to lead poisoning during brain development would, psychometrically, look like a heritable general intelligence. Multiculturalists who expect different cultural groups to have different values and standards of excellence should not expect those groups to be equally represented in all occupations and professions, especially if people are free to enter and leave different lines of work. There is a branch of the wave-function where Margaret Thatcher (trained research chemist and honorary FRS) led a successful push by the international community to address global warming through carbon pricing. (This probably require postponing the collapse of the Soviet bloc by at least a few years, so that her major speech to the UN about the urgency of tackling global warming didn't happen right before the Berlin Wall came down.) In that timeline, pollution charges are regarded as one of the signature policies of neoliberalism. Modern civilization may be doomed because (i) we need to act collectively and globally on climate change, (ii) the USA is the indispensable nation at the center of the network, (iii) the Senate and Electoral College give a veto over American policy to a combination of plutocracy, reactionary folk Christianity and paranoia, and (iv) people like me are unwilling to move to Wyoming, or even West Virginia, to counter this. (I realize there is some tension between this and the previous statement.) A true Burkean conservative in America should work for the preservation and development of the institutions bequeathed us by our wise and heroic ancestors, serving us for half a century, a century, or more: the welfare state; the regulatory agencies; international organizations and treaties; the military-industrial complex; academia; affirmative action; Hollywood and the rest of corporate popular culture. The quantitative social sciences would be in much better shape if the first method everyone learned was $k$-nearest-neighbors , or maybe classification and regression trees , followed by the bootstrap . Linear models and $t$-tests should be, for social scientists , the hyper-mathematical arcana at the back of the textbook which their methods class skipped because there wasn't time. "Prophesying upon the eigenvectors" is more transparently about making stuff up than "interpreting the coefficients", and therefore preferable. There is something very odd about looking at the distribution of node degrees within a network. It makes the network itself into an odd hybrid of a single interdependent object (a relation) and a whole population. Going "something something ergodicity mumble mumble sampling reveals a process grumble grumble shut up and calculate" makes this only a little less weird to me. A good philosophy of probability should explain why all applied Bayesian statistics relies on Monte Carlo, the most frequentist method imaginable. Ideally, it would also explain why Monte Carlo works with deterministic pseudo-random number generators (so the algorithmic information content of the pseudo-random numbers is extremely low). I have toyed for years with the phrases "the simulation interpretation of probability" and "the birth of Trumpism out of the spirit of fandom", but I cannot work out what should stand behind them. (I hope they are unrelated.) Complexity science is a series of footnotes to Norbert Wiener and Herbert Simon . The mythopoetic impulse never goes away , but in populations which have gone through the Flynn / Gellner transition to widespread clerk-ship, it expresses itself not as stories, but as theories which aren't actually explanatory. (It gives us the Oedipus complex, rather than Oedipus.) Every form of progress has its costs. Believing that there was a unique and irreversible transition from viewing time as an eternal cycle to viewing time as unidrectional history is taking sides. His ideas are flawed by a vicious circle; you are engaged in iterative approximation; I stand firm at a fixed point. Dentists are not, in fact, talking their book when they recommend pre-emptive action for wisdom teeth. In a well-functioning social institution, incentives, information and (internalized) norms ensure that it doesn't matter who fills various roles in the institution, it behaves the same way regardless. Institutions are always impersonal. It follows that institutions are information-hiding abstractions, if we're thinking like programmers. But if we're thinking like physicists: institutions are collective degrees of freedom. Blackouts are humanity confronting its own work, and the effects of its own collective actions, as a hostile and alien force. The parable of the Nazi bar is a folk version of the Schelling model . No one should be allowed to opine about artificial intelligence unless they've at least spent an hour or two with ELIZA and then stepped through the code. "Philip K. Dick and the Fake Humans" doesn't yet explain a hell of a lot about modern life, but it will.

title: How I'm thinking about different types of automated alignment
raw_summary: I used to think of "automating alignment" as a natural category. But when I tried to think through the strategic implications, I realised that it depends a lot on the type of work. I'm now thinking of it in three buckets: Empirical alignment research : design and execution of alignment-relevant experiments (for a given notion of what we’re aiming for) Conceptual alignment research: theoretical or judgement-driven work to improve our understanding of what we’re aiming for and how to achieve it (including how to measure it) Direct alignment work : making particular AI systems more aligned (including via inputs such as training data) In the rest of this post I'll walk through my current takes on these in terms what’s needed for automation, how good or bad they look, what our priorities might be (to the extent we're interested in automating alignment [1] ), etc. Automating empirical alignment research This is the most obvious fit for the AI capabilities we’re getting at the moment. You want to know more about the relationship between some alignment-relevant variables? Great, an AI agent can design and run that experiment for you. You want to know what training methods help your alignment benchmark go up? In the not-too-distant future, AI agents will probably be able to do this too. When we have the automated capabilities researchers we seem on track for, this is exactly the kind of thing they’ll likely be able to do a lot of. Note that I’m not counting the design of benchmarks/metrics/evals as part of this bucket. In current practice that’s tightly intertwined with empirical alignment research, and often the hardest part of it. But for automation purposes it clusters much more with conceptual work; it’s easy to imagine automating the rest of empirical research without it (as AI capabilities generally get automated); and I think its automation has different strategic upshots. The capabilities that are needed for automating empirical alignment research very heavily overlap with the capabilities needed for automating AI capabilities research. Therefore, it doesn’t seem like a priority to try to accelerate this type of automation. However, the prospect of getting a lot of automated empirical alignment work before we have good versions of other types of automated alignment work increases the priority of work which complements it. Significantly, that may mean better specification of the kind of numbers we would like measured/targeted. Automating conceptual alignment research What about automating the type of metric choice/construction that we’ve just said would be a good complement to automating empirical alignment work? Or more generally improving our understanding of how to think about alignment, what we’re even aiming for, etc.? This is essentially theoretical research. Automating it is trickier than automating empirical work because of the lack of verifiable signal about what constitutes progress. Accelerating the automation of conceptual research is somewhat fraught (feeding into some dangerous technologies), but seems helpful for a number of high-priority areas, including macrostrategy as well as conceptual alignment work. Overall it seems likely good to do, if we can. Methods for helping to automate conceptual research broadly might include: Curating training data for finetuning Building scaffolds to try to elicit more research progress from current or future models Building methods to extract more signal from existing conceptual research data Building benchmarks for conceptual research capabilities, that can be targeted by AI researchers (or potentially by automated capabilities researchers) Or just identifying good ideas for benchmarks, even if they aren’t fully implemented Automating direct alignment work As well as learning more about what it takes to make systems more aligned , sometimes we want to just make our actual systems as aligned as possible . This overlaps with empirical alignment work, but the emphasis is different: Empirical alignment work is science Direct alignment work is engineering Automating direct alignment work could include a lot of activities which leverage scalable cognition for alignment-relevant purposes. This could include careful auditing of particular RL environments or training data, or direct monitoring/supervision of systems during training. RLAIF for alignment properties is a form of automated direct alignment work; Claude 3 Opus’s apparent self-alignment was another (albeit accidental in that case; but if we knew how to reproduce or generalize the behaviour perhaps it could happen deliberately). I think that the limit of automating direct alignment work would be a form of system 2 learning , where updates are not made blindly towards a training objective, but reflectively by an AI system that was already sufficiently aligned (not necessarily having robustly good values already — just enough genuine care about being aligned, and honesty with itself, that its reflective updates tend to move it further in that direction), and wished to become more so — whatever the deep true version of aligned should mean [2] . Embarking on such a path could be fraught (because of difficulty in being confident that the starting conditions were in the right basin of attraction), but compared to other alignment approaches, it has the benefit that it might leverage the full strength of the AI’s cognition to help, so that its “self-improvement” in an alignment direction is a closer analogue to meditation than to self-performed neurosurgery. So, accelerating the automation of direct alignment work could include: Designing (and analysing) setups that can deploy AI labour to help with direct alignment work Designing paradigms (that could then be tested empirically) that allow AI to be a more active participant in its own alignment Producing data (or scaffolds) to help improve AI taste at the alignment-relevant tasks necessary for this Interactions These categories blur and interact in a number of different ways: Automated direct alignment techniques may be good subjects for empirical experiments This is not completely reliant on having good metrics for alignment; developing a science of what’s going on with different attempts at automated direct alignment could be useful even if we don’t yet know what “good” looks like Automated hill-climbing might get you to very strong direct alignment approaches — but this does rely on having good enough metrics i.e. we could plausibly be in a regime where we’re better at reasoning about and implementing training setups that in fact lead to aligned systems than we are at accurately measuring their alignment. In that case, optimising for our best alignment metrics might produce worse alignment outcomes than following our best-guess direct alignment process. If you can do a good job of automating conceptual alignment research, you should be approximately done (“winning” on the alignment challenge) Since that should then be able to do the relevant parts of prep for automating the other types of alignment work, and being appropriately confident in your techniques for them You could also in principle do a good enough job at direct alignment that the systems you’re building are entirely safe But I think it will be hard to have very strong confidence in that before improving our automation of the conceptual side; and so each new generation of AI might pose a challenge — will your alignment techniques transfer, or will your luck run out? So: the main goal (from an existential risk perspective) for automating empirical research and direct alignment work is to get our systems safe enough to robustly avoid catastrophe (“not losing”) for long enough that we can automate conceptual alignment research to a very high quality level There will likely be approaches that allow you to leverage automation of empirical research to get better automation of conceptual work e.g. Taking Talkie or another LLM with only vintage tra…

title: Delaying Internal Deployments Until After X Days of Safety Testing
raw_summary: This post reflects my own takes, and not that of my employer's. This is a simple idea: before a new model can be deployed internally, you must first test it for a minimum, fixed period. You can adjust various axes of this proposal: Duration of the wait: in calendar time, or until you fulfill some condition. What it blocks: external deployment, internal deployment, or the training of future checkpoints. When the fixed period starts: from the first checkpoint, the final checkpoint, or any checkpoint that is “sufficiently similar / representative” to the one that is ultimately deployed. One concrete target that I like is: “No checkpoint may be used internally for purposes beyond safety testing, until at least X calendar days after its hash is filed with an auditor.” This is one specific implementation of internal deployment lags, an idea that the AI Futures Project (AIFP) briefly discusses in How to pace the US frontier as “AI R&D can only be conducted or assisted by AIs that were trained at least 9 months ago”. What does this look like when implemented? Let’s run through a scenario to pin down the details of this proposal. The places where it could go wrong are in the open questions at the end. A legislative body sets a minimum waiting period of X calendar days (starting at 10 and possibly ratcheting up to 90). No checkpoint in a covered model family may be used internally, beyond safety testing, until X calendar days after its hash is filed with an auditor. Continuing to train a checkpoint’s own weights does not count as internal use. The alternative is for the wait to also block the training of checkpoint N+1, and not just the internal use of checkpoint N. I didn’t go with this because it incentivizes developers to pull out fewer checkpoints for testing, and because delaying training results in an algorithmic overhang. More capable models start exhibiting problems that are harder to surface in short periods (e.g. swarms, long-horizon, memory), so X should possibly increase over time. A model family becomes covered as soon as any of its checkpoints (pre-, mid- or post-trained) is substantially more capable than the last model to complete its wait. If the developer initially claims that the model is not covered but later finds that it is, they will be subject to some penalty (to be determined). There is also an absolute floor on capabilities, so that this doesn’t apply to lots of benign models. In an emergency, the auditor can authorize one named checkpoint to be used early, only for responding to a specific incident (e.g. a harmful model is already causing damage, and the developer has just trained a patched model that could counter it). The standards/legislative body confirms or revokes this within [X days]. The developer continually pulls checkpoints throughout the training process. They first send an auditor a hash, a short fingerprint of the exact weights; then, they carry out safety testing for X days before deploying a checkpoint broadly internally without the below rules. All work has to be fully transparent to auditors. Options for how the X days are structured: Staged testing Stage 1, first part of X: pre-registered evals and named testers in an isolated environment. Stage 2, second part of X: broad monitored internal use, but the model can’t launch jobs, merge code, write to training data, or touch prod. Parallel, hidden runs: whenever someone at the developer uses a cleared model, the new checkpoint gets the same task in a separate sandboxed copy of the environment. Its outputs go only to monitors and the safety team, never back to the person who asked. Open questions The rule itself Should we also allow capability testing? What about ML R&D tasks? One way to game this is to register thousands of tasks from your open R&D backlog, and call running them a capability eval. The outputs are real research (e.g. a faster kernel), and even if you ban using them, people still have to read the transcripts to grade them, so they learn what worked. Pre-registering evals doesn’t help, since it fixes the task list in advance but doesn’t check whether the tasks are live problems. You might end up needing a compute cap. Should we give exemptions for doing safety research? This is an important crux to ask alignment researchers about. Without an exemption, safety research is done with a model that is X days behind, but a blanket exemption lets capabilities work pose as safety work. Should a safety fix (e.g. more post-training, or redoing RL from an earlier checkpoint) restart the X-day wait? It would be bad if it did, as Avi Brach-Neufeld points out here . A developer that finds an issue on day 8 of testing loses more time than one that finds it on day 2, so the rule penalizes finding and fixing problems during the wait. This is probably tolerable at small X, but gets worse as X increases. If safety fixes don’t restart the clock, however, developers could just call capabilities training “safety”. What is the principle behind how much X increases? How large is the risk that an emergency clause would be abused? Concerning behaviours aren’t necessarily caught during pre-deployment testing windows, and are often caught through subsequent monitored internal use. How much are we willing to trade off the value of catching some misaligned behaviours via monitoring internal deployments, vs. being able to pace internal R&D? Which models are covered How is “substantially more capable” defined: effective compute, or something like the Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI)? How would an auditor check that the developer has faithfully stuck to the “more capable” definition? How do you avoid bringing classifiers built using a frontier model into scope? Can a developer keep using earlier checkpoints from a family after it becomes covered? A developer could train a second model family and keep it just under the “substantially more capable” line, so it’s never covered. Researchers could then use that family right away, while use of the main family is on hold. This only gets them so far, since coverage is measured against the last model to complete its wait, and an uncovered family never completes one, so the second family can only be ahead by the “substantially more capable” margin. This becomes a bigger problem if the capability measure itself can be gamed. Gaming the wait How can we stop a developer from using a checkpoint for acceleratory AI R&D work during the wait, by labeling that work as an allowed activity (i.e. any AI R&D task whose output gets used for anything other than testing that checkpoint)? How can we cleanly separate out safety testing from other activities? A developer could give a new model a real task during training, such as writing faster training code, and then use that code to train other models before the new model has completed the X-day wait. A developer could make every researcher an A/B tester, so that they use the new model for normal work and rate its answers, and the developer calls this training. Similarly, a developer could have an RL environment that is just how well the model does actual work inside the company. In stage 1 of staged testing, you run the risk that named testers run large agent swarms for capabilities work, in which case the only difference is that there are fewer humans in the loop. This is probably somewhat mitigated by pre-registering evals, but it’s difficult to still allow AWT. In stage 2, you can still copy paste model outputs into training data, or into code and research plans. A developer could also store outputs from the wait and use them the day the checkpoint clears, without breaking any rule. Should there be a blanket ban on training on outputs from the wait, and how would anyone check? In stage 2, how will you detect if the model is launching jobs, merging code, writing to training data, or touching prod? Developers can game the wait by making lots of models and testing all of them at once, s…

title: Q3.5 Timelines Update: Looks Like the Intelligence Explosion Will Happen in 2027 After All
raw_summary: We want to get this post out quickly given the urgency of the topic. It’s possible that there are some errors in the modeling, but we think it’s very unlikely that they undermine the high level conclusions. We would love to be corrected on any mistakes we made. METR recently estimated that Anthropic is now making AI progress about twice as fast as its historical rate (they would not be surprised by anything from 1.3x to 3x), and guessed that “perhaps ≈80%” of the current acceleration is due to AI. If they’re right, that implies an AI-driven acceleration that is 5 months ahead of the AI 2027 scenario . This level of acceleration due to AI is very unexpected. Previously, Daniel, the most bullish of us, assigned a 50% chance of Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) [1] before 2029 . SAR is roughly the point at which a company would rather fire all their human researchers and rely solely on automated AI researchers than have a team of the best human researchers in the world with no AIs. [2] Now, all of us forecast that Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) will likely arrive at some point in 2027 (assuming no substantial deliberate slowdown). [3] We also predict a 35-65% chance that Top-Expert-Dominating AI (TED-AI), AIs that can automate all white-collar work, will arrive before 2028. While there were many factors and sources of evidence that influenced us, the single biggest source was the METR report. [4] . If SAR is coming in 2027, it is incredibly urgent to pause or substantially ‘pace’ frontier AI development, with the ideal being an industry-wide pause followed by an international agreement . Companies are not on track to align a SAR, and using a misaligned SAR to do recursive self-improvement (RSI) will put us in an extremely bad position. Additionally, if we train SAR in the near future, China will probably be able to steal the training recipe and maybe even the model weights ( more ). [5] Timelines/Takeoff Update Summary We estimate that METR’s report implies a 1.7x AI-attributable acceleration in the pace of progress today, relative to historical levels. This surprises our model; we made our most recent timelines forecasts less than three months ago, and even the most aggressive model-based distribution (Daniel’s) assigned less than 4% to the pace of progress being sped up by at least 1.7x in November 2026. [6] 1.7x AI-attributable acceleration is a bigger deal than it may seem; e.g., it’s a much bigger deal than making employees 1.7x more productive . We focus in this post primarily on forecasting when Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) will arrive. We also discuss Top-Expert-Dominating-AI (TED-AI): AIs that are better than top human experts at virtually all tasks. ( more ) In this post, we forecast SAR and TED-AI using the following approaches: Simple models: Research taste linear extrapolation : Even assuming that the recent pace of progress doesn’t accelerate further due to automation, the fact that the recent trend is above historical rates is a big update to our timelines; a linear extrapolation of the recent rate of AI progress predicts that SAR will likely be achieved by the end of 2027. Labor uplift extrapolation : An exponential extrapolation of self-reported labor uplift predicts SAR in mid-2028. In addition to not modeling automation, there are reasons to think that an exponential is too conservative. However, self-reports may be too bullish. Extrapolating Anthropic automation levels : Anthropic recently shared a graph showing how the percentage of R&D tasks at various automation levels has changed over time. Extrapolating this predicts SAR in late 2027; this method also doesn’t model speedup from automation. Extrapolating software R&D uplift per unit of ECI : AI software R&D uplift must have recently been increasing by a larger factor with each ECI point. If we linearly extrapolate the rate at which this “factor of extra uplift per ECI point” is increasing, we get SAR in Dec 2027 (if we assume that the self-reported AI labor uplift chart is accurate) or July 2027 (if we assume that there was no meaningful automation 12 months ago and all the speed-up has happened after then). Tom Davidson’s toy model: Predicts superintelligence in around a year conditional on a software-only singularity, so SAR sometime in 2027. Filtered AI Futures Model (AIFM) : Keeping the existing AIFM (including parameter distributions), and filtering for trajectories that match METR’s AI-attributable pace of progress acceleration estimates. This serves 2 purposes on top of the simple extrapolations: Modeling how automation changes the rate of progress, allowing forecasting reasonably beyond SAR. Informing what parameter settings in the simple research taste extrapolation are plausible. The results of these methods: How to think about these results: The simple research taste extrapolation, which is a simplified version of the AIFM, gives July or September 2027, depending on whether you account for parameter uncertainty. Other simple models predict late 2027 to mid-2028. When conditioned on 1.7x Nov 2026 AI-attributed acceleration, the AIFM predicts a SAR median of Feb 2027. This is faster than the simple research taste extrapolation because it usually has a higher level of Sep 2026 research taste (in the median case, matching a median researcher), [7] and it accounts for further automation. When additionally conditioning on a 1.2x May 2026 AI-attributed acceleration, predictions get slower because it indicates a lower rate of growth than is typical when only conditioning on 1.7x in Nov. We then explore hypotheses for why the AI Futures Model was wrong , including parameter adjustments and modeling changes. The analysis is highly preliminary, and we were unable to come to strong conclusions. Our top candidates for what explains where we went wrong are: Near-AC coding skills result in more AI R&D uplift than we anticipated . This could explain the combination of ~1.7x AI-attributable acceleration in Nov and (very roughly) ~1.2x in May, without AIs already having high enough research taste to contribute to the acceleration. In this case, the gradual acceleration no longer implies a low research taste slope, so steeper slopes and faster taste-driven takeoffs are more likely. Skills besides coding and research taste (the two included in the AIFM), e.g., data generation, are driving acceleration. This potentially would have similar implications to the above bullet. But it’s unclear. Conversion of uplift to pace of progress is too conservative. I.e., we modeled diminishing returns to AI research effort too harshly. This would point toward a faster takeoff. Here’s an example trajectory from the AIFM showing how things might go if the cause of our prediction error was underestimating AI R&D uplift from near-AC coding skills: [8] After discussing some other considerations , we share our all-things-considered forecasts (conditional on AGI projects/companies not slowing down): Note that the gap between a person’s SAR median and TED-AI median is not their median time from SAR to TED-AI. Because the distributions of the time until SAR and of the time from SAR to TED-AI both have long right tails, the difference of the medians is typically larger than the median of the difference, so subtracting the two columns tends to overstate the median time between the two milestones. METR’s estimates imply that progress is currently sped up by 1.7x due to AI In METR’s recent assessment of AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic , they estimate that, over the past year, AI R&D progress has accelerated by ~2x relative to the trend before Oct 2025. METR estimates that ~80% of current acceleration is downstream of AI (as opposed to other factors), which implies a 1.7x acceleration due to AI (1.67–1.74x depending on how the 80% is read; see appendix ). title: Where is all the AI safety research uplift?
raw_summary: (Thanks to @Goutham Nalagatla for discussion and for sitting with me and talking about it while I wrote it.) METR recently released a report estimating that Anthropic is getting an overall 1.7x acceleration in AI capability progress as a result of AI accelerating their work. As many have noted (see e.g. Ajeya’s post ), this 1.7x acceleration implies that research is being sped up by much more than 1.7x; Ajeya speculates 10x (which is similar to the ~12x uplift estimated by Anthropic staff). That is, this result implies that researchers are producing about 10 times as many quality-adjusted results as they would without AI progress, or as they were a year or two ago. Anthropic researchers estimated that Mythos 5 caused 5x uplift, and we have access to Opus 5.5, which is somewhat better. (I didn’t take their estimate that seriously at the time, because it was quite unclear how the estimate was produced and it seemed very surprising (see Ryan’s discussion at the time), but I’m taking it more seriously now as a result of it being consistent with the METR report). If this is the case, then AIs speed up AI safety research as much as AI capabilities research, we might expect Anthropic safety researchers to be working 10x faster, and external safety researchers to be working 5x faster now and 10x faster soon. And external safety researchers can probably scale compute use faster than Anthropic capabilities researchers can . For example, we at Redwood are well-funded and would totally 5x our compute spend if we had 5x as many experiments to run, unlike Anthropic capabilities researchers who are presumably already doing a pretty good job of using all the compute they have. So I think that we should expect a 5x labor acceleration to turn into more like a 5x research project acceleration. I don't think our empirical research has been going 5x faster since we got access to Fable/Opus 5.5; I would have guessed more like 2-3x speedup. Why is this? Maybe we suck and have not adopted AI as effectively as Anthropic capabilities researchers have. This might be the case. Obviously, Redwood researchers extensively use AI agents for their research, mostly using Claude Code and recently Claude Tag. We also have an in-house scaffold for autonomous AI research, which has produced results that we've published in the past (e.g. here , here ), though we haven't put a lot of work into using or improving this scaffold in the last few months. We found that this research scaffold is pretty good at doing empirical research, but Claude sometimes makes extremely unhinged choices that invalidate its results and is also pretty bad at writing up its findings; these weaknesses substantially reduced how quickly we could use it to produce useful research outputs. If Anthropic had scaffolds that made their models drastically more useful, I expect they would have turned them into products? Maybe they get a lot of uplift from Anthropic-specific infra for their AIs? Maybe they don’t release scaffold features that are specifically useful for ML research? Overall, I think this is maybe a partial explanation, but it seems sort of surprising for our uplift to be way smaller than Anthropic’s. It’s really felt like fundamental weaknesses of the models, rather than scaffold limitations, are the main reason that they haven’t been more useful to us. To some extent, our work is probably less accelerated by AI than Anthropic capabilities research is. I think most of our empirical research is similarly well-suited to AI speedup to most published ML capabilities research. Maybe Anthropic capabilities research is particularly well suited to AI speedup compared to most ML research? Some of the pretraining work may rely more on the AI's strengths. This could be the case if, for example, a big blocker on running experiments on new architectures is implementing them efficiently. One person from Anthropic told me recently that they think that capabilities research is notably more sped up than most of their short-term alignment work. Maybe we've become much more bottlenecked on research judgment, and I haven't noticed? A lot of the research we do is conducted by interns or relatively junior staff who work fairly closely with their manager to prioritize future experiments. Maybe it's the case that our IC researchers are, in fact, going way faster, but this just means they're much more bottlenecked by their managers' time to understand what they're up to. And maybe this is more true of us vs Anthropic because more of their ICs are more senior/self-reliant, or their research requires less tricky judgement? There are some cases where huge speedup happened. E.g. my guess is that Ryan’s work in the Hugging Face investigation was made wildly faster through his intense use of AI agents; this speedup was partially due to the project being pretty amenable to massive agent use (because it involved reading lots of stuff) and partially due to Ryan being experienced with insane agent workflows. Whatever the case is, I feel like we are imminently going to learn a lot about how feasible it is to accelerate AI safety research using AI labor. If empirical AI safety is going to be drastically sped up by AI, that should translate into a huge increase in the rate of valuable outputs from external AI safety researchers very soon. At the very least, if we don’t see huge speedups on the kind of AI safety work that is most amenable to huge speedups, I’m going to think the researchers doing that work are doing something wrong. See also AI speeds up 3rd party safety researchers by ~1.6x (via self-reports) Discuss

title: Ajeya: AI is dramatically accelerating AI research right now
raw_summary: Earlier this week,  Anthropic stated in their S1  that they “may imminently meet” the threshold of “dramatically accelerated progress due to AI” as defined in their Responsible Scaling Policy. In  their latest RSP (effective July 2026) , say this threshold will be met when: They observe or expect overall capabilities progress to be going twice as fast as the fastest sustained rate before AI was contributing much to AI R&D. This is plausibly attributable to AI automating AI R&D, rather than acceleration in compute or other inputs. For the last few months, some of my colleagues at METR have been working on a deep-access investigation to understand how much Anthropic is being accelerated by its AI systems.  From my reading of  their report  and Anthropic’s RSP, it looks like the “dramatic acceleration” threshold has already been crossed. The report authors found that: Between October 2025 and October 2026, capabilities progress at Anthropic has been going about twice as fast as it had been over the previous twelve months. The measurement they report is an internal version of the  Epoch Capabilities Index called AECI; a wide range of other supporting evidence for acceleration has been redacted. They said that this redacted evidence was "a majority of the evidence [they] found most informative." While the pace may have initially started picking up for a mix of reasons, AI automation is probably the large majority of the reason why capabilities are  still  improving at this faster pace today. Their reasons for believing this have been redacted. This is a much bigger deal than it might sound at first. I think this report is the most important update we have gotten about AI risk in the last couple of years — much bigger than  the Hugging Face attack . Naively, it points toward much shorter timelines than most external researchers (including  the AI 2027 team ) have projected. Importantly,  if AI   is roughly doubling capabilities progress overall, it must be speeding up human researchers by  much  more than that. title: Notes on Take-Off Speeds and RSI
raw_summary: I created these notes for use when I facilitate AI safety courses. I'm sharing these notes early because this issue is topical and I suspect it is better to make an imperfect version available early rather than a much more polished version available later. Please note: some of this content was taken from Additional Course Context . I decided recently that the content on take-off speeds really belonged in the same document as the content on RSI, so I'll be releasing an new version of Additional Course Context at some point (to avoid spamming LW, it'll likely be Substack only ; none of my work is paywalled). Some of the other content was taken from Notes on “We’re in Triage Mode for AI Safety”. Miles' article has been removed from the governance course, so I was looking for a new home for this content. I wanted to include it in a document that was intended to be shared in all the courses I facilitate. Take-off Speed: In Take-off Speeds Rules Everything Around Me , Ajeya describes three scenarios: Whilst there isn’t a strict definition of fast vs. slow takeoff, possibly the most influential definition comes from Paul Christiano . Back in 2018, Paul was arguing that a slow takeoff was more likely, “There will be a complete 4 year interval in which world output doubles, before the first 1 year interval in which world output doubles. (Similarly, we’ll see an 8 year doubling before a 2 year doubling, etc.)“: I’ll observe that many people wouldn't call that a "slow" takeoff! At risk of oversimplifying, Paul argued that we should prima facie expect a slow takeoff because someone will generally figure out how to produce a “slightly worse” version of AI before someone figures out how to build the better version (he claims this is supported by the historical record of technological development overall). Yudkowsky disagreed (2021), criticising the intuition that “design precursors with 95% of the technology should at least have 10% of the impact. He writes: “An awful lot of my model of deployment lag is adoption lag and regulatory lag and bureaucratic sclerosis across companies and countries” and “My mainline view is that growth stays at 5%/year and then everybody falls over dead in 3 seconds and the world gets transformed into paperclips” How should we characterise progress up until now? Eliezer writes : If Hanson or Christiano or Karnofsky etc etc believed this was what a "slow takeoff" looked like, they failed to convey that to their reassured, cheerful audience. Tom Davidson responded : If you thought this was what fast takeoff looked like, you also failed to convey that For reference, Eliezer previously defined a fast as meaning, “a timescale of weeks or hours rather than years or decades”. Paul Christiano has shortened his timelines recently. He says he was "broadly right" that "crazy smart AI is preceded by slightly less smart AI, and the gap is a few years rather than a few months", but nonetheless, AI is moving much faster than he predicted ("I've underestimated the pace of progress multiple times before and never seriously overestimated it"). He now predicts 30% chance of a Top-Human-Expert-Dominating-AI within 12 months if we “go full speed ahead”. He writes: And even if we ignored the possibility of accelerating progress on deep learning, we'll soon be in the regime where if there was a much cleverer way to build AI systems that humans haven't thought of (which honestly seems more likely to not) then an AI working for a week is more likely to find it than the last 60 years of human progress. “Bumpy” intelligence explosions Forethought defines an additional scenario . For example, imagine if AI dramatically accelerates algorithm progress for a while, but then this plateaus whilst we figure out how to make robots that can automate the construction of chip fabs. (Modified version of Forethought diagram.) In contrast, Arvind Narayanan (of AI as a Normal Technology ) argues any RSI we do achieve will be narrow (that is jagged): ie. progress on verifiable tasks will continue “for a few more years” or even accelerate whilst progress on unverifiable tasks more or less remains “frustratingly hard”. Elsewhere they’ve framed this as jaggedness applying not just to capabilities, but also to rate of change. (Modified version of Forethought diagram.) “How did you go bankrupt?” Two ways. Gradually, then suddenly.” ― Ernest Hemingway, The Sun Also Rises “Gradually, then suddenly” feels like an underrated possibility to me. Argument in favour: perhaps there’s a phase transition when human researchers are no longer bottlenecking AI development. Argument against: improvements in AI-assistance might be continuous and required simply to maintain the trendline in light of decreasing marginal returns. Delving into the weeds Whilst this is arguably less relevant these days, take-off speeds is distinct from timelines. Take-off speeds are about how fast an intelligence explosion occurs if/when it happens whilst timelines are about when a particular milestone is achieved. Both slow-takeoff/short-timelines and fast-takeoff/long-timelines are conceptually possible. Complicating matters further, if someone talks about short-timelines to AGI, it matters hugely whether they mean human-level intelligence (like some researchers have argued that we have already achieved ) or whether they mean a system that is strongly capable of autonomously learning and improving itself. As Ajeya notes , someone might have short-timelines to AGI and then a slow-take off from there, or they might believe that things will move very fast once we’ve achieved the AGI milestone. A fast take-off post-AGI is much more likely if we mean the latter definition. Of course, whether a “take-off” is fast or slow may depend on when we start counting from. Do we start counting from ChatGPT/GPT4 or only when we hit a particular AGI milestone? Feedback loops The previous section focused primarily on what RSI might look like in terms of outputs , this section focuses on what kind of feedback loop might be driving this. Types of “Intelligence Explosion”: Forethought examines three kinds of feedback loops : Building on top of this, Forethought defines three kinds of intelligence explosion: software only recursive self-improvement AI-technology: driven by improvements in software and chip design, full-stack where AI also helps increase the production of chips. The reason why each type of intelligence explosion includes the previous factors is that they’ve ordered the factors by expected lead-time. If an intelligence explosion is possible, fast takeoff vs. slow takeoff likely depends heavily on what kinds of intelligence explosion would be sufficiently powerful to trigger it. For example, a fast takeoff is much more likely where a software-only explosion is possible, however, if you need to automate the full-stack, then there’d be a much stronger argument for a slow takeoff. We already saw their model of how these different feedback loops could combine depending on the strength of each. I imagine they would have moved a reasonable amount of their probability mass from the “gradual” world to either “rapid” or “bumpy”. They observe that the feedback loops could be divided further: Indeed, the AI Futures model focuses on the possibility of a software intelligence explosion and distinguishes automating coding from automating research. They define the following milestones (see the diagram above for estimated speed-up) where the operationalisations all imagine that we “drop” the AI into the present day: Automated Coder (AC). An AC can fully automate an AGI project’s coding work, replacing the project’s entire coding staff Operationalisation: as productive on their own as only human coders with no AIs (max resource utilisation: 5% of compute).
